--- title: "Estimating EIR from prevalence" --- A parasite survey gives prevalence. The transmission model requires an EIR, so `estimint` inverts the one into the other, returning the EIR that would have produced the prevalence you measured. The inversion does not run on prevalence alone. The model takes six covariates describing the setting alongside it. ## The prevalence model Load it by name. The model is bundled in the wheel, so the call is offline and takes milliseconds. ::: {#b5dad1f3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from estimint import load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model prev_model = load_xgb_model("prevalence") prev_model["features"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['dn0_use', 'Q0', 'phi_bednets', 'seasonal', 'itn_use', 'irs_use', 'prev_y9'] ``` ::: ::: All seven columns are required. Six of them describe the setting, and the seventh, `prev_y9`, carries the driving input. | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a net. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1 | | `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed | | `seasonal` | 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal | | `itn_use` | ITN coverage, 0 to 1. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `irs_use` | IRS coverage, 0 to 1 | | `prev_y9` | Parasite prevalence in the deployment year, 0 to 1 | A missing column raises a `ValueError` naming it. `prevalence` is accepted as an alias for `prev_y9` and copied across for you, which is convenient, because it is also the column name `estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` expects. `run_xgb_model` takes the frame and the model, and returns a plain NumPy array. One element per row. ::: {#108b32a0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} setting = dict( dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82, seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0, ) one = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": 0.30}]) eir = run_xgb_model(one, prev_model) type(eir), eir ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (numpy.ndarray, array([13.39696895])) ``` ::: ::: A prevalence of 30% in this setting implies about 13.4 infectious bites per person per year. ## The shape of the relationship Holding the setting fixed and sweeping the prevalence shows how the EIR behaves. ::: {#76418e99 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sweep = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75]] ) sweep["eir"] = run_xgb_model(sweep, prev_model) sweep[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.05 1.47
1 0.10 2.87
2 0.20 6.79
3 0.30 13.40
4 0.45 28.82
5 0.60 64.22
6 0.75 158.88
``` ::: ::: The EIR is nowhere near linear in prevalence. Doubling prevalence from 0.30 to 0.60 does not double the EIR but raises it roughly fivefold. Between 0.60 and 0.75 the EIR more than doubles again. ::: {#31b0244c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np grid = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in np.linspace(0.05, 0.75, 71)]) grid["eir"] = run_xgb_model(grid, prev_model) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(grid["prevalence"], grid["eir"], color="#00d4aa") ax.set_xlabel("Prevalence") ax.set_ylabel("EIR (infectious bites per person per year)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Inferred EIR against prevalence, holding the setting fixed.](estimating-eir_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='A line rising slowly from near zero at 5% prevalence then climbing very steeply above 60% prevalence, reaching about 160 infectious bites per person per year at 75%.'} ::: ::: Precision in the prevalence you supply therefore matters far more at the top of the range than at the bottom. An input that is a few points out at 70% prevalence moves the inferred EIR by tens of bites per year. ## The role of the setting If EIR were a function of prevalence alone, a lookup table would do the job and no model would be needed. The district in the running example has a measured prevalence of 0.45, pyrethroid resistance of 0.30, and pyrethroid-only nets. In the sweep below the net coverage is the only quantity that varies, and the measured prevalence is held at 0.45 throughout. ::: {#e7fee30e .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import calculate_dn0 rows = [] for coverage in [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]: nets = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=coverage) rows.append({ "coverage": coverage, "dn0_use": nets.dn0, "itn_use": nets.itn_use, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "irs_use": 0.0, "prevalence": 0.45, }) nets_vs_eir = pd.DataFrame(rows) nets_vs_eir["eir"] = run_xgb_model(nets_vs_eir, prev_model) nets_vs_eir[["coverage", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
coverage dn0_use itn_use prevalence eir
0 0.0 0.000 0.0 0.45 22.536
1 0.3 0.311 0.3 0.45 24.170
2 0.5 0.311 0.5 0.45 26.461
3 0.7 0.311 0.7 0.45 31.960
4 0.9 0.311 0.9 0.45 37.058
``` ::: ::: Every row reports the same prevalence. The inferred EIR rises by roughly two thirds across the column. That is why understating `itn_use`, the error described in [Nets and dn0](nets-and-dn0.qmd), biases the inferred EIR downwards. It is also why the same measured prevalence in two districts with different net coverage does not imply the same transmission. ## The global model Passing the model to every call is repetitive. `set_global_model` registers one as the default, after which `run_xgb_model` may be called with the frame alone. ::: {#bc0f9d10 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import set_global_model, get_global_model set_global_model(prev_model) run_xgb_model(one) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([13.39696895]) ``` ::: ::: `get_global_model` returns whatever is registered, or `None` if nothing is. ::: {#d3960d2f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} get_global_model()["class"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` 'estiMINT_model' ``` ::: ::: That is a convenience for interactive work. In a script that touches more than one of the three models, pass the model explicitly. The global slot holds exactly one, and a stray `set_global_model` elsewhere in the session will change what an unqualified call resolves to. ::: {.callout-note} ## The valid range `prev_y9` is clamped to `[0.005, 0.80]`. Values outside that band are quietly pulled to the nearest edge, and no warning is raised. ::: {#d05af444 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.001, 0.005, 0.80, 0.95]] ) edges["eir"] = run_xgb_model(edges, prev_model) edges[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.001 0.894
1 0.005 0.894
2 0.800 234.882
3 0.950 234.882
``` ::: ::: A prevalence of 0.001 and one of 0.005 return the same EIR, as do 0.80 and 0.95. The model reports nothing unusual. If a sweep of prevalences produces an implausibly flat EIR at either end, the cause is almost always this clamp rather than the epidemiology. ::: ## Next - [EIR and HBR](eir-and-hbr.qmd) — the same inversion from entomological data instead. - [Mosquito density and EIR](mosquito-density.qmd) — what happens to the EIR when the vector population changes.
